title: Working Scientifically
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Working Scientifically Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: AC9S5I01, AC9S5I02, AC9S5I03, AC9S5I04, AC9S5I05, AC9S5I06
standard_text: Pose questions and make predictions; plan and conduct fair tests, identifying variables and safety; use equipment to measure and record data in tables and graphs; identify patterns; evaluate methods; and communicate findings (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Year 5 science inquiry content descriptions).
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on working scientifically: testable questions, predictions, fair tests and variables, measuring, averages, graphs, anomalies and conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one thing, measure one thing.
key_sub: A fair test changes one variable, measures one and keeps the rest the same.
body_html:
How to think about it

Scientists ask questions they can test, then plan a fair test.

  • Change one variable, measure one variable, and keep everything else the same.
  • Measure with the right equipment and units, repeat the test, and record the results in a table.
  • Look for a pattern, check results that do not fit, and write a conclusion that matches the data.
Example

Does ramp height change how far a car rolls? What do you change?

the question names the ramp height

Answer: the height of the ramp

Example

Results: 24 s, 26 s, 25 s. Average?

24 + 26 + 25 = 75

75 ÷ 3 = 25

Answer: 25 s

Common mistakes

  • Changing more than one variable at a time.
  • Using a column graph for data that changes over time (use a line graph).
  • Leaving out a result that does not fit without testing it again.

faq.a: A fair test changes only one variable, measures one variable and keeps all the other variables the same, so you know what caused the result.
Repeating a test shows whether the results are reliable. If one result is very different, test again to check it.
Use a column graph to compare separate groups, such as kinds of birds. Use a line graph when something changes over time or when both variables are numbers.

items.q: What should a good prediction include?
c: what you think will happen and why
items.e: Use what you know.

items.q: Why is a fair test important?
c: so the result is what you predicted
so you know the change you made caused the result
so everyone gets the same mark
items.e: Only one thing changes.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the length of a lever affect the force needed to lift a load?" What should be measured?

the force needed to lift the load
items.e: Measure the result (the dependent variable).

items.q: Investigation: "Does the type of surface affect how far a toy car rolls?" What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the same car, the same ramp height and letting go without pushing
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: A table has the heading 'Time'. What is missing?
items.e: Always write units in table headings.

items.q: Investigation: "Does the material of a wrapping affect how fast an ice cube melts?" What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?

items.q: Investigation: "Does the amount of sunlight affect how tall a sunflower grows?" Which variable should be changed?

items.q: Which variable do you measure?
items.e: It is the result.

items.q: Which is the safest way to heat water in a classroom test?

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing how the length of a shadow changes during the day?
items.e: Column graph: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: Which conclusion matches the data: 'the bigger the jar, the longer the candle burned'?

Small jars make candles burn longer.

items.q: A result does not fit the pattern. What should a scientist do first?

items.q: Kai finds one result much bigger than the others. What should he do?
